flashcards.q: Define safe and idempotent precisely, and list which verbs qualify for each.
flashcards.a: Safe: no intended server-side side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE). Idempotent: N identical requests produce the same server STATE as 1 (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE). Safe implies idempotent; idempotent does not imply safe.

flashcards.q: Why is PUT idempotent but POST is not, by definition?
flashcards.a: PUT is defined as 'store this representation AS the entire target resource' -- an end-state statement, so repeating it is a no-op by construction. POST is defined as 'create a new subordinate resource' -- repetition is definitionally the opposite of a no-op, since each call creates something new.

Not by default (RFC 5789 deliberately doesn't claim it is). Depends on the specific operation encoded in the patch document: 'set field to X' twice is idempotent in practice; 'increment field' twice is not.

flashcards.q: What's the network-layer retry rule that follows from safety/idempotency?
flashcards.a: Safe/idempotent methods (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE) are safe to retry blindly on ambiguous failure. POST and non-provably-idempotent PATCH need a client-generated Idempotency-Key so a retry can't cause a duplicate side effect.

flashcards.q: How must an idempotency-key check be implemented to be correct under concurrency?
flashcards.a: Atomically -- reserve the key BEFORE executing the operation (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, checking affected-row count), never read-then-write. Naive read-then-write races when two retries arrive near-simultaneously and both pass the existence check.

flashcards.q: 401 vs 403 -- what's the distinction and why does conflating them break clients?
flashcards.a: 401 = no valid authentication (correct response: authenticate/refresh token). 403 = authenticated but not authorized (re-authenticating won't help). A client treating every 403 as 'token expired' loops refreshing a token that was never the problem.

flashcards.q: Why do 307 and 308 exist when 301/302 already redirect?
flashcards.a: 301/302 predate a strict method-preservation guarantee, and browsers historically rewrote a POST to a GET when following either, dropping the body. 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) are explicitly specified to preserve both the original method AND body across the redirect.

flashcards.q: How do ETags enable both caching and optimistic concurrency from one mechanism?
flashcards.a: Caching: If-None-Match on GET, matching ETag -> 304 with no body. Concurrency: If-Match on PUT/PATCH, matching ETag -> write proceeds; mismatch -> 412 Precondition Failed, preventing a silent lost update (compare-and-swap via headers).

flashcards.q: Strong vs weak ETag validators -- which is safe for optimistic concurrency?
flashcards.a: Strong validators guarantee byte-identical representations on a match; weak validators (W/"...") only guarantee semantic equivalence. Only strong validators are safe for compare-and-swap (If-Match) write safety and for range requests.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between Cache-Control: no-cache and no-store?
flashcards.a: no-store: never persist the response anywhere. no-cache: CAN be cached, but must revalidate with the origin before every reuse -- misleadingly named; it doesn't mean 'don't cache', it means 'don't reuse without checking first'.

Serves the stale cached copy immediately (zero added latency) while asynchronously revalidating in the background for up to N seconds; the next request gets the fresh copy. Trades a bounded staleness window for consistently low latency.

flashcards.q: Why is 429 retryable when most other 4xx codes aren't?
flashcards.a: Most 4xx mean the request itself is malformed/invalid -- retrying identically fails identically. 429 means the request was valid but rate-limited; it should carry a Retry-After header telling the client exactly when to retry, making it a scheduling instruction rather than a fatal error.

flashcards.q: What does a 304 response actually contain, and why does that matter for server cost?
flashcards.a: No body at all -- just a signal that the client's cached copy is still current. For expensive-to-generate resources, the real savings is the server-side generation work itself, provided the ETag is computed from something cheap (a version column, updated_at) rather than requiring a full render first.

flashcards.q: Idempotency is a property of server state, not of the HTTP response. Give the classic example that trips people up.
flashcards.a: A repeat DELETE on an already-deleted resource may return 404 instead of the first call's 200/204 -- the response differs, but the resource state ('it doesn't exist') is identical either way, so DELETE is still idempotent.

flashcards.q: GET is cacheable by default -- is POST ever cacheable?
flashcards.a: Yes, but only with explicit freshness information in the response, and it's rarely used in practice; GET remains the default cacheable method and the one caches are built to optimize for.
